articles.title: Tram Services Disrupted Between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre on Saturday
articles.excerpt: No trams will operate between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre until 2pm on Saturday, 5 September, due to improvement works. A bus replacement service will be in place for affected passengers.
articles.content_html:
On Saturday, 5 September, tram services will be suspended between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre until 2pm due to scheduled improvement works on the Rochdale line. Passengers are advised that a bus replacement service will operate between the affected stops during this time.

Additionally, on Sunday, 6 September, from the start of service until 11am, there will be service changes across the network due to works at Deansgate-Castlefield and Trafford Bar. Travellers should plan accordingly as these changes may affect their journeys.

For those using the Derker tram stop, the lift is currently out of service, and step-free access is available via a ramp from Cromford Street. Passengers heading towards Manchester can access the Manchester-bound platform directly, while those travelling towards Rochdale will need to use the track crossing.

Passengers requiring step-free access at the Failsworth tram stop should note that both lifts are out of service due to replacement works. They are advised to travel to Hollinwood to connect to services. For further assistance, customers can contact the Metrolink contact centre at 0161 244 1000, available from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends.

articles.title: No trains between Rochdale and Manchester Victoria this week as replacement buses run
articles.excerpt: Passengers travelling between Rochdale and Manchester Victoria are being advised to allow extra time this week, with trains replaced by buses from Monday 10 to Friday 14 August.
articles.content_html:
Rail passengers travelling between Rochdale and Manchester Victoria are facing disruption this week, with no train service operating on the route from Monday 10 August to Friday 14 August 2026 because of planned engineering work.

Rail replacement buses are operating between Manchester Victoria and Rochdale. Passengers can use a direct replacement service or a stopping service calling at Moston, Mills Hill and Castleton. Travellers making the full journey between Rochdale and Manchester Victoria are advised to use the direct replacement bus where possible.

The disruption has prompted concern locally after passengers checking journeys discovered that their usual trains had been replaced. One post in the Rochdale Borough Noticeboard Facebook group said: ‘Just noticed there are no trains from Rochdale to Manchester this week, only replacement buses.’

The closure forms part of planned engineering work affecting services into and out of Manchester Victoria. Other Calder Valley services are operating to revised timetables, so passengers travelling beyond Rochdale should check their individual journey before setting off.

Replacement buses generally take longer than the normal rail journey and passengers should leave additional time, particularly during busy commuting periods. Anyone with onward connections is advised to check the latest timetable before travelling.

The disruption is currently scheduled to continue through Friday 14 August, with passengers advised to check National Rail or their train operator for the latest journey information before setting off.

articles.title: New Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig visits Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Newly elected Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today as she begins work across the city-region following her victory in last month's mayoral by-election.
articles.content_html:
Newly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today, bringing the new city-region mayor to the borough during the opening days of her term.

Craig was elected at the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election on 30 July, succeeding Andy Burnham after his return to Westminster. She became the first woman to hold the Greater Manchester mayoralty.

The visit puts Rochdale among the places receiving early attention from the new mayor as she begins the job of representing all ten Greater Manchester boroughs.

At the time of publication, no detailed public itinerary or standalone press release about today's Rochdale visit had been published on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority news pages. Rochdale Daily has checked publicly available material from the mayoral and GMCA press operation and will update this article if further details, photographs or statements are released.

Craig arrives in Rochdale having campaigned on a platform that included expanding the Bee Network, freezing bus fares and extending free bus travel to young people aged 11 to 18. She has also placed housing, economic growth and reducing inequalities among the central issues facing Greater Manchester.

Those priorities are particularly relevant to Rochdale, where transport connectivity, town-centre investment, housing and access to opportunity remain major local issues.

Before becoming mayor, Craig led Manchester City Council from December 2021 and held Greater Manchester responsibilities for economy, business and inclusive growth. She was awarded an OBE in March 2026 for services to local government.

Her election followed the departure of Andy Burnham from the mayoralty. Craig won the contest after the count proceeded to a second round, defeating Reform UK's Sian Astley.

Today's Rochdale visit will therefore be watched for signs of how the new mayor intends to translate her city-region promises into action for individual boroughs outside Manchester city centre.

Rochdale Daily will add any confirmed detail released by the mayor's press team about the purpose of the visit, people she met or commitments made while in the borough.

articles.title: This week in Rochdale, 100 years ago: the town captured from the air in August 1926
articles.excerpt: Exactly a century ago this month, aerial photographers captured remarkable views of Rochdale's Town Hall, Yorkshire Street, railway station, Broadfield Park and industrial works — preserving the town as it looked in August 1926.
articles.content_html:
One hundred years ago this week, Rochdale was a very different town — but thanks to a remarkable series of aerial photographs taken in August 1926, we can still see it almost street by street.

The images, held by the Britain From Above archive, show a dense industrial town of mills, railway infrastructure, tramways, terraced streets and civic buildings. They provide one of the clearest surviving visual records of Rochdale in the inter-war period.

Yorkshire Street was photographed from the air in August 1926 under reference EPW016788. The view shows the familiar line of the street threading through tightly packed buildings, with factories, chimneys and terraced housing occupying much of the surrounding landscape. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016788

Rochdale railway station was also captured that month under reference EPW016784. The photograph shows not only the station but the extraordinary concentration of railway sidings, engineering works and industrial premises that once surrounded this part of the town. The archive identifies features including railway works, cotton mills, a goods shed and the Rochdale Canal terminal basin. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016784

Another image, EPW016791, looks across Town Hall Square. It records landmarks that remain instantly recognisable alongside features which have since vanished or changed beyond recognition. Archive annotations identify St Chad's, the Esplanade, Rochdale Post Office, Drake Street, tramcars and the Rochdale War Memorial while it was still under construction. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016791

Broadfield Park was photographed in the same month under reference EPW016782, giving another extraordinary perspective across the civic heart of Rochdale. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016782

The industrial scale of the town is perhaps most obvious in the August 1926 photographs of Fishwick Street. Image EPW016789 records the railway works there, reflecting the huge engineering and manufacturing presence which once surrounded Rochdale's rail network. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016789

Even before that August series, an Aerofilms photograph taken on 6 August 1926 captured Rochdale Road crossing the railway and Rochdale Canal at Slattocks. The image, EPW016440, preserves a landscape where canal, railway and road infrastructure sat side by side — the transport arteries which helped power the borough's industrial economy. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016440

What is striking about these photographs is not simply what has disappeared. It is how much remains legible. The Town Hall, St Chad's, major road alignments and parts of the railway landscape allow modern residents to orient themselves inside a town photographed from an aircraft a century ago.

The photographs also capture Rochdale during a period of profound change. The borough remained heavily industrial, public transport still included corporation tramcars, and mills and engineering works dominated huge areas which today contain housing, roads, offices and redeveloped land.

The Rochdale Observer itself was already a long-established part of town life by 1926, having first appeared in 1856. Its surviving archive means future editions of Rochdale Daily's '100 Years Ago' feature can go beyond photographs and recover the stories residents were actually reading — crime reports, council debates, sport, advertisements, court cases, births, deaths and the everyday incidents which made up life in the borough.

For this first edition, though, the photographs tell their own story. They allow us to look down on Rochdale exactly a century ago and recognise both the town we inherited and the one that disappeared.

Rochdale Daily intends to make 'This Week in Rochdale — 100 Years Ago' a recurring history feature throughout the centenary year.

IMAGE NOTE: The historic Aerofilms photographs referenced above are held by Britain From Above. Their terms do not permit commercial reproduction without a separate licence, so Rochdale Daily links readers to the original archive images rather than reproducing them without permission.
articles.right_to_reply: Local historians, heritage groups and residents with documented Rochdale material from 1926 can contact news@rochdaledaily.co.uk for future editions of the series.

articles.title: Rochdale's biggest event returns this Saturday as Feel Good Festival takes over the town centre
articles.excerpt: Thousands of people are expected to descend on Rochdale town centre this Saturday as the borough's biggest annual event returns with headline performances from Gabrielle, Ash and Starsailor alongside a packed programme of live music, street food and family entertainment.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's biggest and most attended annual event returns on Saturday 8 August as the Feel Good Festival once again transforms the town centre into one of Greater Manchester's largest free celebrations of live music, food and entertainment.

Thousands of visitors are expected to flock to Rochdale throughout the day, with the stunning backdrop of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall providing the setting for a packed programme of performances, street food and family activities.

Headlining this year's main stage in Town Hall Square is BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, whose career has produced chart-topping hits including Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She will be joined by legendary Northern Irish rock band Ash and indie favourites Starsailor, alongside performances from The Allergies, Alex Spencer, K-STATE, Metro and Dave Sweetmore.

Away from the main stage, live music will continue throughout the day inside venues across Rochdale town centre, with pubs, bars and independent venues hosting local artists and emerging talent, creating a festival atmosphere across the borough.

The festival officially opens at 11:30am, with entertainment continuing throughout the afternoon and evening before the headline performances conclude at approximately 10:45pm.

One of the festival's biggest attractions remains its popular Food and Drink Village, where visitors can enjoy everything from gourmet burgers and pizzas to international street food, loaded fries, desserts, artisan coffee, ice cream, licensed bars and locally produced drinks. Independent traders from across the region will once again showcase a wide variety of food and beverages throughout the day.

Visitors travelling by car are encouraged to use Rochdale town centre's public car parks, including those at Number One Riverside, Rochdale Exchange Shopping Centre and nearby council-operated facilities. Due to the popularity of the event and temporary road closures, organisers recommend arriving early or making use of public transport wherever possible. Rochdale Railway Station, Rochdale Interchange and the Bee Network Metrolink stop are all within a short walking distance of the festival site.

The event has been designed to be accessible for everyone. Step-free routes are available throughout the main festival site, accessible toilets are provided, designated accessible viewing areas will be available near the main stage and British Sign Language interpretation will accompany selected performances. Festival stewards will also be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors requiring additional support.

Since launching in 2008, the Feel Good Festival has welcomed internationally renowned artists to Rochdale and has become one of the North West's premier town-centre music festivals. Beyond the entertainment, it provides a significant boost to the local economy, with restaurants, cafés, bars, shops and hotels all benefiting from the influx of visitors.

Whether you're heading into town to sing along with Gabrielle, relive the guitar anthems of Ash, enjoy Starsailor's iconic hits or simply spend the day sampling fantastic food while supporting local businesses, the Feel Good Festival promises another unforgettable celebration of everything Rochdale has to offer.

articles.title: Taxi driver issues safety warning after frightening incident near Littleborough railway station
articles.excerpt: A taxi driver has shared details of a frightening incident near Littleborough railway station in the hope of encouraging colleagues to remain vigilant while waiting for bookings.
articles.content_html:
A taxi driver has urged colleagues across Rochdale borough to remain vigilant after describing a frightening encounter while waiting for his next booking near Littleborough railway station.

The driver said the incident happened shortly after completing an Uber journey from Rochdale Railway Station to a passenger drop-off in Littleborough. After finishing the fare, he parked on a nearby street opposite Littleborough Railway Station while waiting for his next booking.

According to the driver's account, a man described as a white British male aged between 35 and 45 approached the vehicle accompanied by a dog. The driver says the man opened the car door without permission before placing the dog inside the vehicle, along with a bag containing unknown items.

When challenged, the driver alleges the man became aggressive and attempted to damage the vehicle by striking one of the windows. Fearing for his safety, the driver immediately contacted Greater Manchester Police while remaining inside the vehicle.

The driver says the alleged aggression continued while he was speaking to police, prompting him to drive to a safer, busier location near Sainsbury's Local in Littleborough, where he waited for officers to arrive.

Police subsequently attended the scene, took a statement and dealt with the reported incident. Rochdale Daily has approached Greater Manchester Police to establish whether any arrests were made or investigations remain ongoing.

Following the incident, the driver shared his experience publicly in the hope of preventing something similar from happening to others working in the taxi trade.

He is encouraging drivers to avoid waiting for jobs in isolated streets where possible and instead use well-lit locations with passing pedestrians or nearby businesses. He also advises drivers to keep vehicle doors locked while waiting for bookings and to contact police immediately if they feel threatened.

Personal safety is an important consideration for taxi and private hire drivers, many of whom work alone at all hours of the day and night. Drivers frequently find themselves waiting for bookings in unfamiliar locations or transporting passengers they have never previously met. Industry organisations have long encouraged drivers to remain aware of their surroundings, keep communication devices readily available and report suspicious or aggressive behaviour promptly.

While incidents of this nature remain relatively uncommon, they serve as a reminder of the challenges faced by those working in the transport sector. For many drivers, particularly those working evening and overnight shifts, staying alert and choosing safe waiting locations forms an important part of their daily routine.

Anyone who witnesses criminal damage, threatening behaviour or any incident where someone feels at immediate risk should contact Greater Manchester Police on 999 in an emergency, or report non-emergency incidents by calling 101 or using the force's online reporting service.

articles.title: Heywood MP congratulates Bev Craig and calls for stronger investment in the north of the borough
articles.excerpt: Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on becoming Mayor of Greater Manchester, with both Labour politicians expected to work together on transport, regeneration and investment priorities across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on her election as Mayor of Greater Manchester, pledging to work closely with the new mayor to secure investment, improve transport and strengthen opportunities for communities across the constituency.

In a public letter following the mayoral election, Blundell said voters had 'reaffirmed their belief that only Labour can deliver on hopes for a fairer Greater Manchester that works for everyone'. She added that she looked forward to working with the new mayor to grow the economic and cultural future of towns including Bamford, Castleton, Heywood, Middleton, Norden and Spotland.

The MP said her priorities remain focused on creating 'a positive future' for both towns and their residents, supporting jobs, culture and regeneration while responding to the wishes of local communities.

Transport featured heavily in her message. Blundell described the current journey from Heywood into central Manchester by public transport as 'unacceptable', saying many young professionals and families need a quicker and more reliable connection to the city. She reiterated her support for extending Metrolink to Heywood, noting that previous commitments had suggested 'spades in the ground' by 2028, and called for continued confidence in delivering the project.

She also welcomed the success of the Bee Network but stressed that towns outside Manchester city centre must not be left behind. Buses and future tram connections, she argued, both have an important role to play in improving connectivity across the constituency.

Blundell highlighted the opportunities presented by the Mayoral Development Corporations planned for Middleton and Atom Valley, describing them as exciting regeneration projects that could combine investment with skills development for both young and older residents. She said it was essential that local people were first in line to benefit from the jobs and opportunities created by future investment.

For residents across Heywood and the wider Rochdale borough, the relationship between the new Mayor and the local Labour MP could prove significant. With both politicians representing the same party, supporters argue there may be greater scope for joined-up working between Westminster, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and local councils when bidding for funding, infrastructure projects and devolved investment.

Whether that political alignment ultimately translates into tangible improvements remains to be seen, but transport projects, regeneration schemes and skills investment are all areas where cooperation between regional and national politicians can help unlock funding and accelerate decision-making.

The timing is particularly important for Rochdale Borough Council. The authority has previously warned of significant long-term financial pressures, with forecasts indicating a funding gap that could reach around £16 million by the end of the decade if additional savings or funding are not identified. While the Mayor of Greater Manchester does not directly control council finances, the Combined Authority plays an increasingly important role in distributing regeneration funding, transport investment, housing programmes, brownfield development grants and skills funding across the city-region.

That means a strong working relationship between the Mayor, local MPs and council leaders could improve the borough's chances of securing external investment for projects that might otherwise place further pressure on local budgets. Investment in transport infrastructure, town-centre regeneration and employment initiatives can help stimulate economic growth, attract private investment and broaden the local tax base over time.

However, the partnership alone cannot solve every financial challenge. Local government funding remains largely determined by central government, while council tax income, business rates and rising demand for statutory services continue to place significant pressure on council budgets across England.

Ultimately, constituents will judge the success of the new political partnership not by the warm words exchanged after the election, but by whether it delivers visible improvements. Faster public transport, investment in Heywood and Middleton, better roads, stronger town centres, more employment opportunities and increased funding for local services are among the outcomes residents will hope to see over the coming years.

With both Elsie Blundell and Bev Craig committed to Labour's vision for Greater Manchester, attention now turns from congratulations to delivery. The coming mayoral term will determine whether that political alignment results in lasting benefits for communities across Heywood, Middleton and the wider Rochdale borough.

articles.title: Reform's strongest showing yet reshapes Greater Manchester politics
articles.excerpt: Labour retained the Greater Manchester mayoralty, but Reform UK's strongest regional performance to date has reshaped the political landscape and established the party as the city's principal opposition force.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester has elected a new mayor, with Labour's Bev Craig succeeding Andy Burnham after winning the mayoral by-election. While Labour retained the office, one of the election's defining stories was the emergence of Reform UK as the city's principal opposition force, with Sian Astley delivering the party's strongest performance in a Greater Manchester-wide contest to date.

Craig secured 309,525 votes in the final round, representing 66.3 per cent of the vote, while Reform UK's Sian Astley received 157,178 votes, or 33.7 per cent. The result followed a second-round count after no candidate achieved an outright majority of first-preference votes.

Astley's campaign marked a significant moment for Reform UK in Greater Manchester. Standing on a platform centred on neighbourhood policing, transparency in regional government, public spending and directing more investment towards towns across all ten boroughs, she introduced the party's message to hundreds of thousands of voters and established Reform as Labour's most significant electoral challenger in the city-region.

The first-preference vote illustrated that shift. Astley secured 111,928 votes, comfortably finishing ahead of every other opposition candidate. While Labour maintained its lead, Reform's result demonstrated that many voters are now looking beyond the traditional political parties, reflecting wider political changes seen across England over recent years.

The election also highlighted the scale of the challenge facing every political party in reconnecting with the electorate. Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the Greater Manchester mayoralty was introduced in 2017. More than three quarters of eligible voters chose not to cast a ballot despite the mayor holding responsibility for transport, policing, housing, regeneration, adult education funding and significant economic investment across the region.

For many observers, that figure raises important questions about public engagement with devolved government. The office of Mayor of Greater Manchester has become one of the most influential elected positions outside Westminster, yet millions of residents continue to feel disconnected from regional politics. Whether the low turnout reflected election fatigue, limited awareness of the mayor's powers or wider political dissatisfaction will no doubt be debated in the months ahead.

Astley's campaign also carried wider historical significance. Had she been elected, she would have become the first woman to serve as the directly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester since the office was created in 2017. Although that milestone was not reached, her candidacy demonstrated the increasing diversity of those seeking senior political office within the city-region.

The campaign itself was notable for the issues it placed at the centre of debate. Reform UK argued for greater scrutiny of Combined Authority spending, more visible neighbourhood policing, improved road maintenance and stronger accountability within regional government. Labour focused on continuing the Bee Network, delivering new housing and building on the devolution settlement developed under Andy Burnham. Voters were therefore presented with two distinctly different visions for Greater Manchester's future.

For Rochdale residents, the outcome will have practical consequences regardless of political preference. The mayor oversees Greater Manchester Police through the Police and Crime Commissioner powers, shapes strategic transport investment including the Bee Network, influences regeneration funding and represents the region in negotiations with central government. Decisions taken over the next four years will directly affect communities throughout Rochdale borough.

Although Labour retains control of the mayoralty, the election demonstrated that Greater Manchester's political landscape is becoming increasingly competitive. Reform UK's performance suggests future elections may no longer be defined by a straightforward Labour contest, with Astley's campaign establishing the party as a credible challenger across much of the city-region.

Attention now turns from campaigning to governing. Bev Craig inherits responsibility for one of England's largest devolved administrations at a time of financial pressure, growing demands on public services and continuing debate over transport, policing and housing. At the same time, Reform UK leaves the campaign with increased visibility, a larger regional profile and the opportunity to build on its strongest Greater Manchester result to date ahead of future elections.

articles.title: Labour Wins GM Election: a narrow mandate, a continuity platform, and a borough still waiting
articles.excerpt: Bev Craig is Mayor of Greater Manchester, elected on the lowest turnout the office has seen and taken to a second round by Reform.
articles.content_html:
Bev Craig takes office as Mayor of Greater Manchester having won 309,525 votes to Sian Astley's 157,178, a second-round margin of 66.3 per cent to 33.7. She inherits transport, policing, housing and skills powers assembled over nine years, and a budget running to billions.

Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the office was created. Craig's total amounts to roughly one in seven of those entitled to vote. That is not a criticism of her — she did not choose the date, and no candidate can compel people to the polls. But it could set the stage for what follows. A mayor with powers of this scale and a base of active consent this narrow should expect close questioning, and would be wise to welcome it.

The contest was also tighter on first preferences than the final figure implies. Neither candidate reached 50 per cent outright, which is why a second count was needed. Reform UK finished second across all ten boroughs at its first serious attempt at this office. Labour has held the mayoralty since it was created; it has now been taken to a second round in its strongest English region.

The substantive disagreement is about continuity. Craig campaigned on carrying forward the programme she inherits — the Bee Network, housing delivery, neighbourhood policing, further devolution talks with government. For Manchester that is a reasonable prospectus. For Rochdale it is the least attractive offer available, because the arrangement now being continued has not worked here. The borough sits at the end of a Metrolink line, with a rail service that has been unreliable for years, contributing to a city-region strategy whose most visible results are concentrated closer to the centre.

There is a fair answer to that, and it deserves stating. Craig's supporters argue that a Labour mayor working with a Labour government is better placed to win further devolved powers and the money attached to them, and that Rochdale gains more from that than from opposition. It is a serious argument. It is also a testable one, and the test is whether the borough's share of transport and housing investment rises over the next four years or stays where it is.

On policing, the mayor holds the powers of a Police and Crime Commissioner, which makes this the area where the office touches residents most directly. Our measure will be simple and public: response times, charge rates, and whether people who report a crime in this borough hear back. Those figures are published. We intend to use them.

The by-election itself carried a cost — the 2024 mayoral contest cost taxpayers £4.7 million, and this one is expected to run to millions again. That is a consequence of a sitting mayor leaving mid-term for Westminster, not of anything the new mayor did. But it is money spent on an election in which three quarters of the electorate did not participate, and it is reasonable to ask what the region got for it.

Craig begins with substantial powers and a quiet electorate. We will report what she does with them, and judge her on what changes in this borough rather than on what is announced in Manchester.

articles.title: Everything You Need to Know Before Rochdale Feel Good Festival 2026
articles.excerpt: From headliners and ticket prices to travel, parking, accessibility and the latest weather forecast, here's everything you need to know before Rochdale Feel Good Festival returns next weekend.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's biggest annual music event returns next weekend, with thousands of visitors expected to descend on the town centre for the 2026 Feel Good Festival. Headlined by BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, alongside indie favourites Ash and Starsailor, the festival promises a full day of live music, street entertainment, food, drink and family activities, continuing a tradition that has become one of Greater Manchester's most successful free town centre festivals.

Now celebrating its 15th edition, the Feel Good Festival has grown from a small local music event into one of the highlights of the borough's cultural calendar. Previous festivals have welcomed acts including Ocean Colour Scene, Razorlight, Feeder, The Coral, Scouting For Girls, The Fratellis, Heather Small, Cast, Toploader, Badly Drawn Boy, The Feeling, The Lightning Seeds and The Beat, attracting visitors from across the North West and providing a welcome boost to Rochdale's hospitality and retail sectors.

This year's main stage takes place in the stunning surroundings of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall Square on Saturday, 8 August. Headlining the evening is Gabrielle, whose catalogue includes classics such as Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She is joined by Ash, Starsailor, funk and soul outfit The Allergies and Manchester indie rising star Alex Spencer, with additional performances throughout the day and live entertainment continuing across numerous indoor venues around the town centre. Most indoor performances remain completely free, with only the main stage requiring a ticket.

Festival organisers have continued their commitment to making the event affordable. Early bird tickets sold out quickly at £15 before subsequent release phases increased to £25, £30, £35 and the final allocation at £45 plus booking fees. VIP upgrades remain available for those wanting premium viewing areas and additional hospitality. Every ticket includes a reusable festival cup as part of the organisers' ongoing efforts to reduce single-use plastics.

Entertainment begins from 11.30am and continues until approximately 10.45pm, with the main stage located in Rochdale Town Hall Square. Festival organisers recommend arriving early to collect wristbands, avoid queues and enjoy the wide variety of free entertainment taking place throughout the town centre before the headline performances begin.

Getting to the festival is expected to be straightforward thanks to Rochdale's excellent public transport links. Organisers are encouraging visitors to use public transport where possible, with Metrolink trams running directly into Rochdale town centre and Northern train services providing regular connections from Manchester Victoria, Leeds, Halifax and Blackburn. Numerous Bee Network bus services also stop within a short walk of the festival site, while taxi ranks will operate throughout the day and into the evening to assist those travelling home after the headline acts.

Drivers are advised to allow extra time, as town centre car parks are expected to fill quickly. Public parking is available at several locations including The Esplanade, Riverside, Baillie Street and other nearby council-operated car parks, although temporary road closures around the Town Hall may affect access during the festival. Visitors are encouraged to check council travel advice before setting off.

Accessibility continues to be a major focus for organisers. A dedicated accessible viewing platform will be available within the main stage arena for wheelchair users and those with mobility issues, while British Sign Language interpreters will be present during main stage performances. Accessible toilets are provided both within the outdoor festival site and nearby indoor venues. Essential companion tickets are available free of charge for eligible visitors, assistance dogs are welcome and a quiet space will also be available for anyone requiring time away from the crowds.

Toilets will be located throughout the festival site, including accessible facilities, with additional public conveniences available inside participating venues. Festival stewards will be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors and provide directions around the event.

Food has become almost as popular as the music in recent years, with dozens of traders expected to serve everything from gourmet burgers and wood-fired pizzas to Asian street food, desserts and locally produced refreshments. Although organisers have not published official bar prices, visitors should expect festival-standard pricing broadly comparable with similar outdoor events across Greater Manchester. Outside alcohol is not permitted inside the main stage arena, although sealed soft drinks and water may be allowed subject to festival rules. Visitors are encouraged to support local independent food and drink traders operating throughout the event.

The weather currently looks favourable for festival-goers, with forecasts suggesting a mostly sunny day, light winds and temperatures reaching around 19°C. While conditions can always change, current forecasts indicate comfortable weather for spending the day outdoors, although organisers still recommend bringing sunscreen, drinking plenty of water and packing a light waterproof just in case the British summer has other ideas.

Beyond the music, the Feel Good Festival has become an important economic event for Rochdale. Thousands of visitors pass through the town centre every year, providing a significant boost to local restaurants, pubs, cafés, hotels and independent retailers. The festival also showcases Rochdale's cultural offer following the restoration of the Grade I-listed Town Hall and supports the borough's wider ambitions to attract more visitors and investment.

The festival is organised on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council with support from Rochdale Development Agency, ticket sales and sponsorship from local businesses and community partners. Over the years, numerous organisations have supported the event, helping to ensure it remains one of the North West's best-value music festivals while continuing to celebrate local talent alongside nationally recognised artists.

For anyone planning to attend, organisers recommend arriving early, using public transport where possible, checking travel updates before setting off and allowing extra time to move between venues. Whether you're there to see Gabrielle, discover new artists, enjoy the food village or simply soak up the atmosphere in Rochdale town centre, this year's Feel Good Festival looks set to continue one of the borough's proudest summer traditions.

articles.title: After Burnham: What the Next Mayor Inherits
articles.excerpt: The next Mayor of Greater Manchester will inherit far more than Andy Burnham's office, taking responsibility for one of England's most powerful devolved administrations at a time of political and financial change.
articles.content_html:
Whoever becomes the next Mayor of Greater Manchester will inherit one of the most powerful devolved political offices in England at a pivotal moment for both the city-region and national politics. Andy Burnham's departure after almost nine years in office marks the end of an era that saw the mayoralty evolve from a relatively new experiment in devolution into a position with significant influence over transport, policing, regeneration, housing and economic development.

Burnham's resignation to return to Westminster has inevitably altered the political landscape. During his time as mayor he became synonymous with Greater Manchester's devolution agenda, frequently acting as the public face of the region during negotiations with successive governments. Whether residents agreed with his policies or not, few would dispute that he raised the national profile of Greater Manchester and demonstrated how influential a metro mayor could become.

The incoming mayor therefore faces a different challenge from Burnham in 2017. Rather than creating the office's identity from scratch, the next incumbent must decide whether to build on Burnham's approach or chart a new direction. Expectations are considerably higher than they were nine years ago because the public now expects the mayor to deliver visible improvements rather than simply establish the role.

Transport remains the most obvious priority. The Bee Network has become one of the flagship achievements of Greater Manchester's devolution settlement, bringing buses back under public control and integrating services with trams and active travel. While supporters argue that the network is beginning to create a genuinely joined-up public transport system, critics continue to raise concerns about reliability, congestion, funding and the pace of implementation. The next mayor will inherit both the opportunities and the political scrutiny that accompany such an ambitious programme.

Policing is another area where expectations remain high. The Mayor of Greater Manchester also exercises the powers of the Police and Crime Commissioner, giving the office direct responsibility for setting policing priorities, overseeing budgets and holding Greater Manchester Police to account. Crime, antisocial behaviour and neighbourhood policing featured prominently throughout the by-election campaign, with candidates from across the political spectrum promising safer communities, stronger visible policing and better support for victims.

Housing and regeneration are likely to remain central themes throughout the next mayoral term. Greater Manchester continues to experience significant demand for affordable housing while balancing pressures for economic growth, environmental protection and infrastructure investment. Large regeneration schemes are transforming parts of Manchester city centre, Salford and several surrounding boroughs, but many communities continue to ask whether the benefits of that growth are being shared equally across the region.

For Rochdale, those questions are particularly important. Investment decisions made by the combined authority influence transport links, skills funding, brownfield regeneration, town centre renewal and wider economic development. Although individual councils retain many planning responsibilities, the mayor plays a significant strategic role in shaping investment priorities across Greater Manchester.

The constitutional picture is also changing. Devolution has steadily expanded over the past decade, with successive governments transferring additional responsibilities from Whitehall to regional authorities. Greater Manchester has often been used as the model for further devolution elsewhere in England, meaning decisions taken by its mayor frequently attract national attention. The incoming mayor is therefore likely to spend as much time negotiating with ministers as delivering local policy.

The by-election campaigns reflected differing views about how those powers should be exercised. Labour argued for continuity, seeking to build on existing transport and regeneration programmes. Reform UK focused on reducing public spending, increasing accountability and prioritising crime and community safety. Restore Britain centred its campaign on transparency, democratic reform and greater public involvement in local decision-making. The Conservatives promoted business growth and improved public services, while the Green Party emphasised sustainability and environmental investment. Liberal Democrats highlighted local accountability and public service reform. Although their policies differed considerably, almost every candidate accepted that the mayoralty has become one of the region's most influential political offices.

Another challenge awaiting the successful candidate is rebuilding public engagement. The record-low turnout has inevitably raised questions about democratic participation. While the mayor's powers have expanded significantly since 2017, public awareness has not always kept pace. Many residents still struggle to distinguish between the responsibilities of local councils, Parliament and the combined authority. Improving understanding of what the mayor actually does may become almost as important as delivering new policies.

Financial pressures will also shape the next administration. Like councils across England, Greater Manchester faces difficult decisions over public spending. Rising demand for public services, inflationary pressures and competing investment priorities mean every major project will come under close scrutiny. The next mayor will need to balance long-term ambitions with short-term financial realities while maintaining public confidence.

Perhaps the greatest test, however, will be leadership. Andy Burnham's tenure demonstrated that a metro mayor can become a nationally recognised political figure capable of influencing debates far beyond the boundaries of Greater Manchester. His successor now inherits not only extensive powers but also heightened expectations. Residents will judge the next mayor not simply by campaign promises but by whether transport improves, neighbourhoods feel safer, regeneration reaches towns beyond Manchester city centre and economic growth benefits communities across all ten boroughs.

The constitutional significance of this transition should not be underestimated. For the first time since the office was created, Greater Manchester is entering a post-Burnham era. Whether that represents continuity or a fresh chapter will depend not only on the election result but on how effectively the next mayor uses one of the most powerful devolved mandates in the country. The office has matured; now its next occupant must prove that devolution itself can continue to deliver meaningful change for the people it was designed to serve.
